winter-park/rodent-control.heroLocal: Winter Park's rodents do not come up from a swamp — they come down out of the trees. A century of live oaks leans over tile roofs and 1920s bungalows from Hannibal Square to the chain of lakes, backyard citrus drops fruit all winter, and every addition, converted garage, and crawlspace seam on those old houses is a seam a roof rat already knows. At ground level the lakes and canals do the same work for Norway rats, working seawalls, docks, and boathouses lot by lot.
winter-park/rodent-control.heroService: Rodent control in Winter Park is exclusion carpentry with trapping attached, done on houses that were never built like new stucco boxes. We ladder the roofline and read the canopy first, trap what is already inside the attic, then close tile ends, soffit gaps, and pipe chases with chew-proof metal that respects original trim and plaster — and we tell you exactly which oak limb is the bridge, because sealing a house and leaving the bridge up just moves the entry point.
winter-park/rodent-control.whyHeading: Why Winter Park roof rats live overhead, not underground
winter-park/rodent-control.whyLead: Listen after 10 p.m. in the historic core and you will hear the pattern: scratching and light running above the ceiling, heaviest where an oak limb touches tile. Roof rats travel the canopy, power drops, and fence tops as an elevated road system between citrus trees and rooflines, and one established scent trail pulls newcomers for months after the first rat is gone. That is why a Winter Park attic with pellets in the insulation is almost never a stray — it is a route with a stop on it.
winter-park/rodent-control.whyLocal: The construction decides the entry. Pre-war bungalows around Park Avenue, College Quarter, and Hannibal Square have been added onto for a hundred years: crawlspaces under the original house, slab under the addition, a converted garage with its own seams, and clay tile ends that were never screened. Mid-century homes in Virginia Heights and Winter Park Pines trade the crawlspace for low rooflines under oak and pine, where soffit vents and A/C line penetrations do the same job. We map your house's version of the seam before we set a single trap.

pests.name: Roof Rats
pests.blurb: Winter Park's number one attic call, and it is almost always a canopy story: oak limbs or palms brushing tile, gnawed citrus left on the lawn, blunt pellets along the attic runs over the kitchen. They chew soffit vents and tile ends wider week by week. We trap in the attic — never poison in insulation — seal the openings with metal, and name the limb to lift so the bridge comes down with the entry.

pests.name: Norway Rats
pests.blurb: The ground-level rat of the chain of lakes. Bigger, heavier, and burrowing — look for burrow mouths along seawalls, under dock boxes and boathouses on Lake Virginia and Lake Osceola, and greasy rub marks at garage corners. They work the shoreline and the Howell Creek low ground, then push into ground floors and crawlspaces. We trap the runs and close the ground-level gaps, not just the roofline.

pests.name: House Mice
pests.blurb: In a 1920s Winter Park bungalow a mouse does not need much: a pencil-width gap around a sink pipe, a plaster wall void, the seam where an addition meets the original house. You find rice-sized droppings in drawers and chewed corners on stored food, and the calls spike when mice push into garages and kitchens for warmth in January. We seal the pipe chases and interior voids and set traps where they actually travel — behind the stove, along the wall lines.

pests.name: Squirrels in the Attic — the Honest Distinction
pests.blurb: Daytime thumping over the ceiling in Winter Park is usually not rats at all — it is gray squirrels coming and going from the oaks at dawn and dusk. We will tell you plainly when the attic noise is squirrels, because the fix is different: one-way exclusion after the young are mobile, then sealing the tile end or soffit they used. Selling you a rat program for a squirrel problem is how attics stay noisy.

pests.name: Rats Around Citrus and Lakefront Food
pests.blurb: Fallen oranges and grapefruit under a backyard tree, a dog bowl on a lakefront patio, birdseed stored in a dock box — Winter Park yards feed rodents within a short run of a roofline. One night of dropped citrus can hold a rat family on a lot for a season. Part of the visit is the unglamorous list: pick fruit the day it falls, bring the bowl in at dark, and store seed in metal, not plastic.

winter-park/rodent-control.processIntro: Traps alone will not hold a Winter Park house the canopy leans on — here is the order that does.

process.detail: We ladder the eaves, check tile ends and soffit vents, read the oak limbs and palms touching the roof, scope the attic for pellets, rub marks, and matted insulation runs, and walk the crawlspace seams and ground-level gaps where additions meet. Every opening gets a photo, so you are deciding from evidence on your own house, not a pitch.

Snap traps and enclosed stations go in the attic and along the runs the rats actually use, out of reach of kids and pets — no poison in insulation, ever, in a house where a dead rat in a wall void becomes a week of smell. We return and shift sets until the night noise stops, then check a beat longer to be sure the route is really quiet.

process.step: Exclusion built for tile and historic trim
process.detail: Tile ends, soffit gaps, pipe collars, and garage corners close with steel mesh, flashing, and sealant rated for Florida heat and gnawing — fitted around original wood trim and plaster instead of smeared over it. We finish with the arborist list: which limbs to lift off the roof and which vines to pull off the wall, because a sealed house under a standing bridge is a temporary fix.

We bag droppings and nesting fluff, wipe stained wood, and flag insulation that is soaked through and holding odor — that scent is what pulls the next rat down the same trail. Then the Winter Park habits that matter: citrus picked the day it falls, trash locked before dark, dock boxes and birdseed in metal, and a recheck after the first big storm pushes new animals around.

localSection.heading: Historic-core attics, chain-of-lakes shorelines, and the mid-century canopy streets
body: In the historic core — Park Avenue, College Quarter, Hannibal Square, Orwin Manor — the rodent work is overhead and architectural. Bungalows and cottages built in the 1920s sit on crawlspaces, wear clay tile, and carry a century of additions, each joint a potential entry a rat can widen. Roof rats run the oak canopy straight onto those roofs, nest over kitchens and primary bedrooms, and leave pellets and gnawed wiring in insulation nobody has looked at in years. We work these houses gently and thoroughly: ladder every eave, screen every tile end, and seal with materials that disappear against the original trim.

On the chain of lakes — the Lake Virginia and Lake Osceola shore, Palmer Avenue, Via Lugano, Genius Drive, the Rollins College waterfront — the pressure splits in two. Roof rats still work the waterfront oaks and backyard citrus above, but Norway rats own the ground: burrows along seawalls, runs under docks and boathouses, dock boxes raided for stored food and seed. Lakefront exclusion that only seals the roofline leaves half the problem standing, so we walk the water side of the lot with the same care as the attic and harden both levels in the same plan.

Out in Virginia Heights, Winter Park Pines, and the streets toward Howell Creek and Mead Botanical Garden, the houses are younger — mid-century ranch and block — but the canopy is not. Low rooflines sit under mature oak and pine, soffit vents and A/C penetrations open the attic, and the creek-side low ground keeps Norway rats and mice moving after heavy rain floods their cover. Winter is the garage season here: mice slip the door seal for warmth, and the first sign is droppings along the wall, not noise. We seal the low game as carefully as the high one, and tell you which of the two your house is actually playing.

winter-park/bed-bug-treatment.heroLocal: Winter Park bed bugs do not arrive through a resort corridor — they arrive in good luggage, in a student's duffel coming home from a semester away, and in a beautiful estate-sale chair nobody inspected before it went into the guest room. This is a town that travels, hosts, and buys old furniture with a past: Rollins families flying in for parents' weekend, guest houses over garages that sit closed for months and then fill for the Sidewalk Art Festival, and 1920s homes full of upholstered antiques. The bugs ride those ordinary, respectable routes and settle into the quietest bedroom in the house.
winter-park/bed-bug-treatment.heroService: Bed bug treatment in Winter Park starts with confirming live bugs before anyone pays, then treating the room the way this town's houses demand: antique frames and plaster walls handled gently, heat used only where old wood, sprinkler heads, and stored instruments say it is safe, and every sleeping surface counted — the primary bed, the guest-house bed over the garage, the daybed in the study, the student's room that stood empty all semester. You get findings in writing, room by room, and a recheck on the hatch interval, not a fog and a hopeful goodbye.
winter-park/bed-bug-treatment.whyHeading: Why Winter Park bed bugs hide in guest rooms, not master bedrooms
winter-park/bed-bug-treatment.whyLead: The pattern here is delay. A guest room, a carriage-house suite, or a college student's bedroom sits closed and undisturbed for weeks, so an introduction from one suitcase or one visiting relative gets a full breeding cycle — sometimes two — before the first sleeper reports bites. By the time anyone calls, the bugs are not new arrivals on one mattress seam; they are established in the frame, the baseboard, and the upholstered chair beside the bed, in the one room nobody enters between visitors.
winter-park/bed-bug-treatment.whyLocal: The houses help them stay hidden. Historic Winter Park construction is full of harborage a new stucco box does not have: plaster-and-lath wall voids, original wood bed frames with a century of joints, built-in cabinetry, and guest suites over garages and in converted quarters that share a wall with the main house but get checked half as often. Add the semester rhythm around Rollins College — move-outs in May, move-ins in August, study-abroad returns in January, shared off-campus houses in College Quarter where furniture passes from one lease to the next — and Winter Park gets fresh introductions on a school calendar, every year.

pests.name: Bed Bugs in Guest Rooms and Guest Houses
pests.blurb: The signature Winter Park call: nobody sleeps in the room, so nobody notices. Look for dark spotting along the guest-bed frame joints, shed skins behind the headboard, and bugs tucked into the guest-house sofa bed that folds the harborage into its mechanism. We inspect the suite over the garage and the study daybed with the same care as the primary bedroom — in this town the spare bed is usually patient zero.

pests.name: The Rollins Semester Introduction
pests.blurb: Dorm rooms, shared off-campus houses, and a semester abroad all end the same way: a duffel and a mattress topper carried into a family home in College Quarter or Hannibal Square and set down in a bedroom. Move-in and move-out weeks are when we confirm the most student-linked cases. The fix is a real inspection of what came home, luggage unpacked in the garage — never on the bed — and treatment of the one room before the bugs find a second sleeper.

pests.name: Estate-Sale and Antique Furniture Bugs
pests.blurb: Winter Park estate sales move gorgeous upholstered pieces out of old homes every weekend, and bed bugs travel in frame joints, tufting buttons, and the underside webbing of a chair that sat in a closed bedroom for years. A vintage find is not a reason to panic — it is a reason to inspect before it crosses the threshold. We check joints and seams with a light and tell you plainly whether a piece is clean, treatable in place, or not worth the risk.

pests.name: Carpet Beetle Larvae — the Usual Suspect That Isn't
pests.blurb: Fuzzy, slow larvae feeding on lint, hair, and wool in closets and under rarely moved beds are Winter Park's commonest bed bug false alarm, especially in older homes with wool rugs and stored blankets. Their shed hairs irritate skin and get reported as bites. No bed bugs means no bed bug bill: deep extraction cleaning, source removal, and storage changes are the treatment, and we put that in writing too.

pests.name: Fleas From the Yard and the Visiting Dog
pests.blurb: The other night-bite call, and the pattern gives it away: bites low on ankles, worst in the room where a visiting family dog slept, in houses where oak-shade yards and lake-walk routes keep fleas moving year-round. A white-sock walk across the carpet separates fleas from bed bugs in minutes. The treatment then targets the animal source and the carpet base — not the bed frame — and we will not sell you the wrong program to avoid the conversation.

winter-park/bed-bug-treatment.processIntro: In houses with antiques, plaster, and a guest suite out back, the careful sequence matters more than the strong chemical — here is the order.

process.step: Inspect every sleeping surface, guest spaces first
process.detail: Primary and guest beds, the suite over the garage, sofa beds and daybeds, plus headboard walls, luggage stands, and the upholstered chair beside each bed. You see the evidence with us, room by room. If it is a look-alike — carpet beetle, flea, roach nymph — we name it and stop there; no treatment is built on a photo of a bite.

process.step: A prep list written for this house
process.detail: Room by room, in plain language: what to launder hot and bag sealed, what to leave exactly where it sits, and how we handle the pieces that cannot take heat or a laundromat run — antique frames, instruments, artwork, and the contents of a guest house that hosts twice a year. Students get the move-home version: what gets inspected in the garage before it ever reaches a bedroom.

process.step: Treat the harborage, matched to old construction
process.detail: Steam and targeted treatment go into seams, frame joints, and baseboard gaps where the bugs actually live. Whole-room heat is used only where the house allows it — we say up front where original woodwork, sprinkler heads, plaster, and stored valuables rule it out, and what we do instead. No foggers: in a multi-room historic house they scatter bugs into wall voids and make the next visit harder.

process.step: Recheck on the hatch interval, with monitors
process.detail: Eggs outlive the first treatment, so interceptors go under bed and guest-house legs and we return on the hatch interval to read them. When counts hold at zero you get the dated clearance in writing, plus the Winter Park habits that keep it that way: luggage off the bed and unpacked in the garage, estate-sale pieces inspected before they come inside, and a seam check on the guest room before festival and holiday visitors arrive — not after they leave.

localSection.heading: Historic-core guest rooms, the Rollins semester cycle, and mid-century family streets
body: In the historic core — Park Avenue, College Quarter, Hannibal Square, Orwin Manor — the bed bug work is a guest-room story. Houses built in the 1920s carry carriage-house suites, converted quarters, and spare bedrooms that host a handful of nights a year: parents' weekend, the art festival, the holidays. An introduction in October can breed undisturbed until Thanksgiving. We work these houses gently and completely — every sleeping surface including the one over the garage, antique frames treated in place where they can be, and a written room-by-room result the homeowner can actually file.

Around Rollins College and the Lake Virginia shore — Palmer Avenue, Via Lugano, Genius Drive, the streets within a walk of campus — the calendar drives the risk. Students come home from dorms, shared houses, and semesters abroad with luggage and soft furniture that goes straight into family bedrooms, and in May and August the same furniture moves between leases in the shared houses near campus. We inspect what came home before it settles in, treat the single affected room hard, and give families the move-in checklist that breaks the cycle next semester instead of repeating it.

Out in Virginia Heights, Winter Park Pines, and the mid-century streets toward Howell Creek, the calls are family-ordinary: a grandparent who travels, a teenager back from a tournament trip, a beautiful secondhand reading chair from a weekend estate sale. These homes catch introductions early more often — somebody sleeps in the room every night — so the work is usually one bedroom done thoroughly, monitors to prove it stayed done, and honest guidance on the chair: inspected, cleared, or not coming inside. Either way you hear it from the inspection, not from a sales script.

orlando/termite-control.heroLocal: Orlando is not one termite market, it's three stacked on the same sandy soil. In College Park, Thornton Park, and Lake Eola Heights you've got 1920s bungalows on pier foundations with heart-pine framing and crawlspaces that stay damp off the lakes. Out in Lake Nona and Horizon West it's slab-on-grade subdivisions barely old enough for their builder pretreats to fade. Between them sit the Conway chain, Belle Isle, and Delaney Park — lakefront streets where the water table sits high enough that a colony never has to travel far for moisture.
orlando/termite-control.heroService: Termite control in Orlando starts with the construction, not the chemical. We crawl the bungalow crawlspaces, probe bungalow sills and bungalow-era trim by hand, sound baseboards and moisture-meter bath and laundry walls in the block-and-stucco homes, and walk slab edges and expansion joints in the new builds. Then we match the fix to what we actually found — bait monitoring, a liquid barrier trenched to the footing, or direct treatment into drywood galleries — and we show you the evidence photos before we quote anything.
orlando/termite-control.whyHeading: Why Orlando's mix of old bungalows and new slabs keeps termites fed
orlando/termite-control.whyLead: Eastern subterraneans need moisture, wood, and undisturbed time, and Orlando hands them all three in every era of housing. The lake chains keep soil damp and crawlspaces humid through the dry season. Daily summer irrigation holds the foundation line wet even when it hasn't rained. Historic homes have had a century to develop the slow leaks, settled grades, and wood-to-soil contacts colonies love — a planter poured against the stucco, a fence run touching the wall, an addition joint that was never flashed. And the new subdivisions start with their own handicap: form boards and wood scraps buried in backfill, grade pushed high against fresh stucco, and pretreat barriers that thin out right as the neighborhood's landscaping matures.
orlando/termite-control.whyLocal: The pattern changes by neighborhood, so the inspection does too. In the historic districts the risk hides under the house — mud tubes on piers, sills softened from below, drywood pellets in original window trim that owners blame on old paint. Around the Conway lakes and Belle Isle, high water tables mean subterranean pressure is constant and Formosan colonies — which can nest in a damp wall void without touching the ground — are a genuine possibility, not a scare word. In Lake Nona and the other growth corridors, the calls come at the five-to-ten-year mark: swarmers in a garage, tubes up a slab edge behind the mulch, right where the builder's pretreat has worn thinnest. We inspect for the pattern your street actually has.

localSection.heading: Bungalow crawlspaces, lake-chain lots, and growth-corridor slabs
body: The historic bungalow belt — College Park, Colonialtown, Thornton Park, Lake Eola Heights, Delaney Park — is where Orlando termite work gets found early or gets expensive. Pier foundations give us crawlspace access, and we use it: sills, joists, and plumbing lines read directly, tubes mapped before they reach the floor system. These houses also carry drywoods in fascia, porch columns, and original trim, so the inspection goes up as well as down. Owners here care about the wood for its own sake, and findings come documented with photos you can hand to a carpenter or a preservation contractor.

Lakefront and lake-chain homes — Conway, Belle Isle, Edgewood, the streets off Lake Davis and Lake Cherokee — combine a high water table with heavy irrigation and, often, older dock and boathouse timber at the water's edge. Subterranean colonies work year-round in soil that never really dries, and the damp-wall conditions Formosans need show up in flat-roof tie-ins, laundry walls, and A/C line chases. We moisture-meter those walls on every lakefront inspection, because an aerial Formosan nest is its own job and a soil-only treatment will walk right past it.

The growth corridors — Lake Nona, Horizon West, Laureate Park, Storey Park, and the new sections out toward Avalon Park — are slab country. There's no crawlspace to read, so the evidence lives at the edges: tubes climbing expansion joints and slab perimeters behind mulch, swarmers appearing in garages and front entries after spring rains, bath-trap and plumbing penetrations where the slab was cut. This is where bait monitoring earns its keep — stations read on schedule catch pressure while it's still outside the house, in the years when the original pretreat is fading and nobody is watching.

pests.name: Eastern Subterranean Termites
pests.blurb: Orlando's default colony, and it works all year in soil this warm and wet. You'll meet it as pencil-thin mud tubes on bungalow piers and block stem walls, frass-free hollow baseboards in College Park and Conway homes, and swarmers pouring out of a mulch bed on the first warm evening after a spring rain. We split tubes to confirm live workers, trace the moisture feeding the run — a shower valve weeping into a wall, grade tipped toward the house, irrigation heads soaking the stem wall — and treat the colony, not just the tube.

pests.name: Formosan Termites
pests.blurb: Formosans run colonies in the millions and, given a damp wall or roof void, can nest above ground without ever touching the soil — which is why a barrier-only treatment can report success while the house is still being eaten. Around the lake chains we hunt the signs on purpose: blistered paint that feels spongy, carton material in wall voids, moisture readings that make no sense for the weather. Find an aerial nest and it gets treated directly, on its own line item, not folded into a soil quote.

pests.name: Drywood Termites
pests.blurb: Drywoods live inside the wood itself and Orlando's older housing stock is full of their favorite lumber: bungalow fascia and porch trim, attic framing in the historic districts, original window and door casings, even hardwood furniture in Lake Eola Heights homes. The giveaway is a neat pile of hard, ridged pellets under a pinhole in painted wood. We probe the piece, clean out the frass, and wait for fresh pellets to confirm the gallery is live before treating it directly — no tenting quote for a problem the size of a door frame.

pests.name: Dampwood Termites
pests.blurb: A dampwood colony is a moisture problem announcing itself. They settle where wood stays wet — a rotted eave under a College Park oak canopy, a sill under a dripping hose bib, fence boards and landscape timbers touching stucco near the lakes. Colonies stay small and slow, and we'll treat what's live, but the honest fix is the repair: dry the wood out or replace it and the colony loses its home. We'll tell you which pieces are that simple and which aren't.

pests.name: Carpenter Ants (the Swarm-Season Look-Alike)
pests.blurb: Every spring, Orlando homeowners bag what they're sure are termite swarmers that turn out to be Florida carpenter ants — pinched waist, elbowed antennae, out after dark instead of at dusk. They don't eat wood; they excavate damp sills, lanai framing, and foam insulation and push out fine sawdust. The wing check takes thirty seconds — uneven wings and a bent waist mean ant — and it matters, because baiting an ant colony and treating for termites are different jobs at different prices. We identify first, in writing, before anyone sells you anything.

process.detail: Crawlspace first where the house has one — sills, joists, piers, plumbing lines — then attic framing, then room-by-room sounding of baseboards and probing of casings. Slab homes get the edge walk instead: expansion joints, bath traps, garage perimeters, and the mulch line. Lakefront walls and flat-roof tie-ins get moisture-metered either way. Every tube, pellet pile, and clean run gets photographed.

process.step: Written findings, active separated from old
process.detail: You get the photos and a plain-English write-up that separates live activity from old damage and both from mere risk factors — the three get priced very differently. Buying, selling, or refinancing in Orlando? The same inspection serves as your WDO documentation for the file, which is how a lot of our historic-district calls start.

process.step: Treatment fitted to the colony and the house
process.detail: Bait stations placed and mapped for monitoring where pressure is building, liquid treatment trenched to the footing where an active subterranean colony calls for it, and direct wood treatment into confirmed drywood galleries — combined per house, and worked carefully around brick streets' root zones, mature oaks, pavers, and original bungalow trim that can't be replaced.

process.step: Monitoring through swarm season and beyond
process.detail: We come back to read stations, re-walk the soil line, and check the spots swarmers favor after the spring and early-summer flights, when fresh wings show what's still active. Sell the house, add a room, regrade a bed, or re-sod against the foundation and we remap the layout on the spot, so coverage never lapses quietly the way a forgotten pretreat does.

orlando/termite-control.processIntro: Termite work in Orlando is inspection-led and house-specific — here's how it runs.

lake-buena-vista/general-pest-control.heroLocal: Lake Buena Vista runs on turnover, and general pest control here has to run on it too. Along Hotel Plaza Boulevard and SR-535 the work is hotels, condo resorts, and restaurant blocks where a kitchen never fully cools down. Off Palm Parkway and Apopka-Vineland it is vacation condos and timeshares that sit empty between stays, then fill overnight. And tucked around Lake Bryan and Little Lake Bryan are ordinary residential streets — single-family homes with lanais, pool cages, and lake-edge oaks — that get the classic Florida pattern and want a classic quarterly barrier, not a hotel logbook.
lake-buena-vista/general-pest-control.heroService: General pest control in Lake Buena Vista starts by sorting which of those three you are, because the treatment is different in each. Managed properties get bait-first interior work, numbered monitors, and a written record a manager can forward. Vacation units get inspected and treated in the empty window between bookings, before a guest becomes the inspection program. Lake Bryan homes get an exterior-first barrier walked around the pool cage, the mulch line, and the soffits. In all three, we show you what we found — droppings, egg cases, a trail behind a coffee maker — before we quote anything.
lake-buena-vista/general-pest-control.whyHeading: Why turnover, shared walls, and wet resort grounds keep Lake Buena Vista buggy year-round
lake-buena-vista/general-pest-control.whyLead: Nothing here ever fully resets. Guest and tenant turnover is daily, so German roaches arrive in grocery deliveries, cardboard, and small appliances, and pharaoh ants are already travelling the pipe chases behind the walls. Kitchens in the dining blocks along SR-535 and Disney Springs stay warm and wet through double shifts, floor drains grow the biofilm drain flies breed in, and a unit left vacant for two weeks in Florida humidity is a quiet, undisturbed home for silverfish and pantry pests in the dry goods somebody left behind. Spraying the room you saw a bug in does not touch any of that — the colony, the chase, and the drain are the job.
lake-buena-vista/general-pest-control.whyLocal: Outside, the grounds are managed to stay lush, and lush is habitat. Irrigation runs whether it rained or not, pool splash and dumpster-pad runoff keep the mulch and the expansion joints damp, and palms and hedges are planted right against the buildings. That is where American cockroaches — palmetto bugs — stage all day before pushing under a service door after a storm, and where ghost ants nest before trailing into a ground-floor bathroom. For the Lake Bryan streets the same pressure comes from the lake edge instead of the loading dock: retention water, oak shade that never dries, and fruit and feeder trees that keep everything fed. We treat the staging ground, not just the sighting.

localSection.heading: Hotel corridors, vacation condos, and the Lake Bryan residential pockets
body: For hotels and condo resorts on Hotel Plaza Boulevard and along SR-535, general service is a back-of-house program as much as a guest-room one. We work the kitchens, laundry rooms, trash-chute rooms, and housekeeping closets where German roaches and pharaoh ants actually live, place and read numbered monitors so a trend shows up in the log before it shows up in a review, and keep guest-room work bait-and-void based — no broadcast spraying in an occupied room, and a service record written for the brand inspection file, not the technician's notebook.

Vacation condos and timeshares off Palm Parkway, Apopka-Vineland, and Vineland Avenue turn over too fast for problems to announce themselves slowly. A German roach egg case in a condo kitchen can hatch out between two bookings; ants can move from a neighbouring unit through a shared chase while the unit sits empty. We schedule inspections and treatment inside the turnover window, check the under-sink voids, appliance motors, and water-heater closets guests never open, and leave the manager a per-unit note — what was found, what was treated, what to watch — so the same unit flaring twice reads as a pattern, not two surprises.

The residential pockets around Lake Bryan and Little Lake Bryan get a different visit entirely. These are year-round homes, many with pool cages and lanais backing onto the water, and the call is usually palmetto bugs in the garage after rain, ghost ants on the kitchen window sill, and spiders webbing the cage corners. We build the barrier outside first — foundation, weep holes, hose bibs, cage seams, and the mulch edge — treat inside only where sign shows, and hand the homeowner the short fixes that matter here: irrigation heads soaking the stem wall, mulch piled over the weep holes, and a palm touching the roofline.

pests.name: German Cockroaches
pests.blurb: The defining general-pest problem of the resort corridor. Germans live inside the building — behind condo refrigerators, inside coffee-maker and microwave motors, under hotel dish machines — and they arrive constantly in deliveries and luggage-adjacent clutter. You'll see pepper-like specks and tan egg cases in cabinet hinges before you see a live roach in daylight. Store spray makes them scatter deeper into the chase. We gel-bait the harborage, work the neighbouring units or stations on the same run, and put the sanitation misses feeding them in writing.

pests.name: Pharaoh Ants and Ghost Ants
pests.blurb: The bathroom-sink and coffee-station ants of Lake Buena Vista. Pharaoh colonies nest inside wall voids across whole condo buildings and bud into new colonies when sprayed, which is why a room can be 'treated' three times and get worse. Ghost ants trail in from the irrigated mulch to ground-floor baths and kitchens. Both get traced to the entry and the moisture, then baited with what they carry home to the colony — and we tell housekeeping and homeowners plainly: no surface spray on the trail, it splits the colony and doubles the map.

pests.name: American Cockroaches (Palmetto Bugs)
pests.blurb: The big outdoor roach of the pool deck, the dumpster pad, and the Lake Bryan garage. Palmetto bugs breed in damp mulch, palm boots, and sewer and drain lines, then push indoors under door sweeps and through pool-cage seams when storms flood their harborage. Killing the one in the laundry room changes nothing. We dust voids and meter boxes, treat the foundation and mulch edge where they stage, and flag the torn sweep or flooded bed that let it in.

pests.name: Drain Flies
pests.blurb: Tiny moth-like flies around a hotel bathroom sink or a restaurant floor drain are not a spraying problem — they are a plumbing-hygiene signal. Drain flies breed in the gelatinous biofilm inside drains, overflow slots, and broken grout lines, so a fly today means a drain that needs scrubbing, not fogging. We identify which drains are producing, treat the biofilm, and write the drain-care fix into the service record, because in a food or lodging inspection that note is worth more than the treatment.

pests.name: Silverfish and Pantry Pests in Vacant Units
pests.blurb: Units that sit empty between owners, seasons, or long bookings grow their own quiet fauna. Silverfish graze book bindings, stored linens, and cardboard in humid closets and water-heater rooms, and Indian meal moths and weevils work through the rice, cereal, and pet food left in a pantry. Nobody sees it until the next arrival opens the cupboard. Vacant-unit checks are part of our turnover inspections: dry goods gone or sealed, closets and voids checked, and light treatment only where sign actually shows.

process.detail: We walk the setting you actually have: guest rooms and back-of-house for hotels, the full unit — sinks, appliances, water-heater closet, lanai — for vacation condos, and the exterior envelope first for Lake Bryan homes. Grounds are part of every version: dumpster pads, dock and service doors, palm lines, pool equipment, and the mulch against the wall. Findings are photographed as we go.

Inside, German roaches and pharaoh ants get gel bait and void work, not broadcast spray — safer around guests and kids, and the only approach that reaches the colony. Outside and in residential work we build the wet-season barrier along the foundation, weep holes, cage seams, and thresholds, and treat drains producing flies at the biofilm, not the air.

Door sweeps, pipe and conduit penetrations, chase gaps, and weep holes get sealed or screened with materials that hold. What belongs to the property — a drain that needs a scrub schedule, a dumpster lid that will not close, irrigation soaking a stem wall, dry goods stored through a vacancy — goes in the written record that day, named plainly, so a manager, cleaner, or homeowner can act on it.

process.step: Rechecks on your calendar, not ours
process.detail: Hotels and dining get scheduled monitor reads, vacation units get rechecked on the booking calendar — ideally each turnover for flagged units, monthly for the rest — and Lake Bryan homes settle onto a quarterly barrier with free re-treatment if palmetto bugs or ants break through between visits. Same-unit repeats get flagged in the record instead of billed as new surprises.

lake-buena-vista/general-pest-control.processIntro: General service in a turnover city is a calendar and a paper trail as much as a treatment — here's how it runs.

lake-buena-vista/bed-bug-treatment.heroLocal: In Lake Buena Vista a bed bug call is rarely about a house — it is about a room that was sold last night and is supposed to be sold again tonight. Along Hotel Plaza Boulevard and SR-535 that room sits in a stack: one above, one below, and a neighbour on each side, with a housekeeping cart rolling past all of them. Off Palm Parkway and Apopka-Vineland it is a vacation condo or timeshare unit a cleaner has just walked into on a turnover. Around Lake Bryan it is a guest bedroom that sat made-up and empty for weeks. Three different buildings, one rule that governs all of them: that room stays out of service until it clears — nobody sleeps in it on a hope and a spray.
lake-buena-vista/bed-bug-treatment.heroService: Bed bug treatment in Lake Buena Vista starts with the room, then immediately widens to the rooms around it. We inspect the bed, the headboard, the luggage rack, and the sofa bed everyone forgets to open, then check the adjoining units and the ones above and below before we quote anything. Hotels get a discreet, unmarked visit and a written record for the brand file. Condo managers get a per-unit note they can forward to an owner who lives three states away. Homeowners get an honest identification first — because in Lake Bryan homes the thing in the guest room is, a good share of the time, not a bed bug at all.
lake-buena-vista/bed-bug-treatment.whyHeading: Why nightly turnover makes Lake Buena Vista a bed bug relay, not a bed bug source
lake-buena-vista/bed-bug-treatment.whyLead: Bed bugs here do not need to breed up a local population — the luggage supply renews them. Every check-in on Hotel Plaza Boulevard brings suitcases that have been in other hotels, other rentals, and airport baggage systems, and every checkout risks carrying the problem to the next property in a cleaner's cart, a laundry bag, or a guest's own bag moved to a fresh room. Moving a complaining guest across the hall without inspecting either room is how one introduction becomes a floor. The work is interception: catch it in the room it arrived in, prove the neighbours are clean, and document both.
lake-buena-vista/bed-bug-treatment.whyLocal: The buildings help them. Hotel headboards are bolted through shared walls, pipe and conduit chases connect stacked bathrooms, and housekeeping closets and linen rooms give bugs warm, undisturbed harbourage between stays. Timeshare and condo buildings on Palm Parkway add a harder problem: nobody owns the pattern. Each unit has a different owner, cleaner, and booking calendar, so the unit above can flare twice while the unit below is never checked. That is why our inspection map is the stack and the row, not the single address on the work order — and why the written record matters as much as the treatment.

localSection.heading: Hotels on Hotel Plaza Boulevard, condos on Palm Parkway, and guest rooms on Lake Bryan
body: For hotels along Hotel Plaza Boulevard and SR-535, the visit is built around discretion and proof. We arrive unmarked, take the flagged room out of service, and inspect it with the adjoining rooms and the units directly above and below, plus the luggage rack, headboard, and housekeeping station serving that section. Treatment is targeted to the harbourage we actually found — bed frame joints, skirting, upholstered furniture — not a whole-floor fogging that scatters bugs into the wall voids. The manager leaves with a dated record: what was found, where, what was treated, and when the room can return to service, written so it can be handed to a brand inspector or attached to a guest claim without editing.

Vacation condos and timeshares off Palm Parkway, Apopka-Vineland, and Vineland Avenue live or die on the turnover window. The person who finds bed bugs here is usually the cleaner, stripping a bed between a morning checkout and an afternoon arrival, and the worst outcome is rushing the unit back for that arrival. We work inside that window when we can and say plainly when we cannot: the unit is held, bedding is bagged at the bed and laundered hot, interceptors go under the bed legs, and the neighbouring units on the shared-wall side get checked on the same visit. Remote owners get the finding in writing with photos, because 'the cleaner saw something' is not a basis anyone can approve a bill on.

The residential streets around Lake Bryan and Little Lake Bryan get the quieter version of the same pest. Here it is a guest room used six weekends a year, a second home that sat closed between visits, or a teenager's room after a season of travel-team tournaments and sleepovers. Bugs can feed once, then sit for weeks with no host and no one looking. We inspect every sleeping surface in the house — including the pull-out in the lanai room — identify what we find before treating, place monitors where the room sits empty, and give the homeowner a simple check to run before the next guests arrive, instead of a standing panic every time someone visits.

pests.name: Bed Bugs in Hotel Guest Rooms
pests.blurb: The classic Lake Buena Vista find: bugs harbouring in the bed frame joints, the bolted headboard, the seams of the luggage rack webbing, and the nightstand drawer runners — within a metre of where the guest sleeps, and nowhere else in the room. Housekeeping usually sees the evidence first: rust-coloured spots on the sheet corners, shed skins along the headboard ledge, a live bug when a mattress is stripped. We confirm it live before any treatment is sold, photograph the harbourage, and treat that tight zone plus the furniture that touches it.

pests.name: The Rooms Next Door, Above, and Below
pests.blurb: A single-room treatment in a stacked hotel or condo building is a half-treatment. Bed bugs travel the wall void on pipe and conduit runs, follow housekeeping carts and laundry bags, and turn up next in the room that shares the headboard wall. Every flagged room gets its cluster checked — both sides, above, and below — and the linen room and cart serving that section get inspected too. If the cluster is clean, that goes in the record; a documented negative next door is what lets a manager defend returning the floor to service.

pests.name: Sofa Beds — the Harbourage Nobody Opens
pests.blurb: In condo resorts, timeshares, and extended-stay suites the pull-out sofa is the bed nobody inspects: folded shut for months, warm, dark, and fed for one night at a time by the extra guest. We have cleared a room's main bed twice and found the living population in the sofa mechanism on the third visit — which is why we open it first now. Sofa beds, upholstered headboards, and recliners within feeding range of a sleeping spot are treated as beds, because the bugs already do.

pests.name: Turnover Finds in Vacation Condos
pests.blurb: In a Palm Parkway condo the discovery moment is specific: a cleaner strips the bed, sees spotting or a live bug, and a new family is due at four. Panic produces the two classic mistakes — spraying the mattress with store product, which drives bugs into the frame and the wall, and remaking the bed and saying nothing. Our cleaners' rule is simpler: stop, photograph, bag nothing, close the door, call. We hold the unit, inspect, and treat inside the changeover if the finding is light — and we tell the manager the same day if it is not a one-visit fix.

pests.name: Carpet Beetle Larvae — the Guest-Room Look-Alike
pests.blurb: The honest entry on this page. Small, bristly larvae and shed skins in a Lake Bryan guest room or a seldom-used hotel room are very often carpet beetles, not bed bugs: they graze wool, feathers, lint, and dead insects in undisturbed corners, they do not bite sleepers, and they do not need a bed bug treatment. Telling them apart takes two minutes with a lens — segmented and hairy versus smooth and apple-seed shaped. If it is beetles, we say so, point at the source material to remove, and do not sell you the treatment on this page.

process.step: Out of service, then inspect the cluster
process.detail: The flagged room or unit comes off the market first. We then inspect every sleeping surface in it — beds, sofa beds, upholstered headboards — with a light and a lens, and extend the check to the adjoining rooms and the units above and below, plus carts and linen storage serving that section. You get the map of what was found and what was cleared before treatment is discussed.

process.step: Prep written for a turnover, not a textbook
process.detail: Bedding comes off into bags at the bedside, never carried loose down a corridor, and goes to a hot wash and hot dry. Luggage stays off beds and gets inspected on the rack or in the bath. For condos, the prep sheet goes to the cleaner and the manager in writing with the hold time stated; for hotels, housekeeping gets the five-minute strip-and-check that catches the next introduction at the sheet, not at the review.

process.step: Treat the harbourage that was found
process.detail: Treatment is matched to the evidence: targeted application into frame joints, headboard voids, skirting, and furniture seams where bugs were confirmed, interceptors under bed legs, and mattress encasements where the property wants them. No broadcast fogging of an occupied floor, no treating clean neighbouring rooms 'just in case' — the cluster record says which rooms needed it and why.

process.step: Clearance recheck before the room is sold again
process.detail: Eggs hatch on their own schedule, so a room is not cleared on treatment day. We recheck on the hatch interval — monitors read, harbourages re-inspected — and only then issue the clearance note: hotels get it for the brand and claim file, condo managers get it per unit for the owner, and Lake Bryan homeowners get monitors left in the quiet guest room with a date to check them. If the recheck finds activity, the room stays held and retreatment is on the original job.

orlando/rodent-control.heroLocal: In Orlando a rat call is usually a canopy call. Over College Park, Thornton Park, and Conway the live oaks never really break — limb touches limb touches roofline, with a power line or a cable run filling any gap — so a roof rat can cross a whole street without once touching the ground. Under that canopy sit 1920s bungalows with open eaves, louvered attic vents, and detached garages that were never sealed to modern standards. Across town the problem flips: downtown, International Drive, and the UCF corridors feed Norway rats and house mice at ground level around dumpsters and shared walls, and out in Lake Nona and Horizon West the newest slabs in the city are still getting their first rats pushed in off the pond banks and the next construction phase.
orlando/rodent-control.heroService: Rodent control in Orlando starts above your head, not in your kitchen. We walk the canopy and the roofline first — which limbs touch, which lines land on the roof, where the eaves and vents have been gnawed — then read the attic for runs, rub marks, and pellets, and only then work the ground: garage seals, AC line penetrations, dumpster and dock areas. Trapping removes what is inside, exclusion in steel and flashing is what keeps the next rat out, and you get the entry map in photos before we quote the seal work. We do not scatter poison through an attic and call the smell that follows a solution.
orlando/rodent-control.whyHeading: Why Orlando's canopy, lakes, and growth keep rats fed all year
orlando/rodent-control.whyLead: Roof rats need three things — food above the ground, water nearby, and a covered route between them — and Orlando's older neighborhoods hand over all three on the same lot. Mature oaks drop mast through the fall, old backyard citrus and loquats fruit on trees nobody harvests anymore, and the lake chains and retention ponds mean no rat is ever far from water. There is no winter kill to reset the population: breeding slows, it never stops, so a gap gnawed in October is a litter by the new year. Add a housing stock full of pier foundations, additions, and century-old vent screens, and the surprise is not that an Orlando attic has rats — it is that one stayed empty this long.
orlando/rodent-control.whyLocal: The route in changes completely by neighborhood, so the inspection does too. Under the historic canopy the rat travels high — fence, line, limb, roof — and enters at the top of the house, which is why ground baiting alone never fixes a College Park attic. Around the restaurant rows, apartment complexes, and hotel back-of-house areas downtown and on International Drive, the pressure is at ground level and shared: one dumpster pad feeds every unit on the wall, and mice move through pipe chases from kitchen to kitchen. In the growth corridors the rat is a displaced field animal — construction clears the lot next door, the pond bank gets regraded, and Norway and cotton rats arrive at brand-new garage doors whose seals were never fitted tight. Same city, three different animals' worth of behavior, three different jobs.

localSection.heading: Canopy bungalows, shared-wall corridors, and brand-new slabs
body: The historic canopy belt — College Park, Thornton Park, Colonialtown, Delaney Park, and the Conway streets — is roof rat country, and the work there is measured in limbs and eaves. We start in the street looking up: which oak limbs overhang or touch the roof, which utility drops land on it, where the fronds of a palm lean against a tile edge. Inside, the attic tells the story in rub marks along the top plates, pellets clustered under the AC handler, and trails worn through blown insulation between the entry point and the water lines rats gnaw for moisture. These bungalows also carry detached garages, carriage houses, and additions tied into the original frame with gaps nobody has looked at since the addition was young. We trap on the mapped runs, then seal the top of the house — eave returns, vent screens in hardware cloth, gnawed corners rebuilt in flashing — and give you the honest limb list: which cuts actually break the route and which are just tree work.

Downtown, along International Drive, in MetroWest, and around UCF, rodent work is a shared-wall problem and it lives at ground level. Norway rats work the dumpster pads, grease areas, and loading edges behind restaurants and apartment buildings, burrowing under pads and slab edges, then running the wall lines into ground-floor units. House mice ride the same buildings from the inside, traveling pipe chases and the voids behind stoves, which is why one unit's kitchen problem keeps reappearing two doors down. Treating a single unit in that pattern is a subscription to the same call. We inspect the wall, not just the address: the pad, the burrows, the door sweeps on the whole run, and the pipe penetrations in each kitchen, and we put the findings in writing a property manager can act on — because half the fix in these buildings is the pad and the doors, not the traps.

Lake Nona, Laureate Park, Horizon West, and the lake-chain edges south through Belle Isle and Edgewood show the third pattern: new houses, new rats. The slabs are tight but the garage doors often are not — a corner gap where the seal meets an uneven apron is a front door to a mouse and a young rat — and AC penetrations and hose bibs get sealed with foam that rodents treat as a snack. Around the houses, retention ponds, regraded banks, and the construction phase still clearing lots next door push Norway and cotton rats toward the first finished streets, while pool equipment pads, screen-enclosure doors, and boathouse and dock timber along the Conway lakes give roof rats harborage that never gets checked. We fit and replace garage seals properly, collar the utility penetrations in materials that hold up to gnawing, screen the equipment and enclosure gaps, and walk the pond-facing side of the lot with you so you can see exactly where the pressure is coming from and what trimming and cleanup actually changes it.

pests.name: Roof Rats in the Oak Canopy
pests.blurb: Orlando's signature rodent, and an aerial one. Roof rats run the oak limbs, fence tops, and utility lines over College Park and Conway after dark, drop onto roofs, and enter through gnawed eave corners, lifted tile edges, and louvered vents whose screens gave up years ago. You hear them between ten and two — light running, a thump, scratching that moves — and find blunt-ended pellets and dark rub marks in the attic where the run crosses a joist. Fallen citrus and unpicked loquats in the yard are the fuel. We trap on the runs the attic map shows, seal the top of the house in steel and flashing, and mark the limbs that have to come off the roofline to break the route.

pests.name: Norway Rats at Ground Level
pests.blurb: The big, ground-dwelling rat of the dumpster pad, the lake bank, and the pond edge. Norways burrow — look for fresh dirt and a clean hole under a dumpster pad, a slab edge, a boathouse floor, or along a retention bank in Lake Nona — and they travel low, leaving greasy rub along walls and garage edges where the run touches the building. Around International Drive and the apartment corridors they are a building-level problem fed by one pad; in new subdivisions they are the animal pushed in when the lot next door gets cleared. We map the burrow system, trap the runs, and fix the pad, door, and seal failures feeding them — a burrow system next to an open food source refills as fast as it is emptied.

pests.name: House Mice in Shared Walls
pests.blurb: A mouse needs a gap the width of a pencil, and Orlando's apartments, condos, and rental rows are full of them — around sink pipes, behind stoves, at the tub access panel, where the AC line enters. Rice-sized droppings in a drawer or along the back of a counter, a chewed corner on a dry-goods box, a faint scratching inside a wall at night: that is the whole first chapter. Because they travel the chases between units, mice are the rodent most often mistreated as a single-apartment problem. We find and seal the penetrations in your unit, trap behind the appliances where they actually run, and tell you plainly when the pattern says the wall itself needs the building treated.

pests.name: Rats Around Pools, Docks, and Equipment Pads
pests.blurb: Lake-chain and pond-side homes give rats a second address outside the house: the pool equipment pad, the screen-enclosure frame, the boathouse and dock timber, the outdoor kitchen. Roof rats harbor in pump housings and hollow dock framing, run the enclosure top rail to the roofline, and raid the fruit and pet food that live out by the lanai. Owners hear nothing indoors and assume the droppings by the pump are a lizard until the gnawing reaches the equipment wiring. We inspect the outdoor structures as part of the house, screen and seal the housings and enclosure gaps, and treat the lanai-to-roof connection most services walk straight past.

pests.name: When It Is Not Rats at All
pests.blurb: An honest Orlando rodent call starts with admitting how often the noise is something else. Grey squirrels run bungalow attics by day — heavy, diurnal, and loud at first light, where rats are creatures of the night. Flying squirrels slip through gaps too small for rats and work quietly after dark in the older canopy streets. A raccoon in a chimney or a torn soffit is a bigger, slower sound entirely, and bats in a vent show as staining and guano, not gnaw marks. Each one is a different job with different rules, and trapping for rats you do not have fixes none of them. We identify what is actually up there from the sign — pellets, rub, entry size, timing — and say so before anything is sold.

process.detail: We start in the street looking up — limbs on the roof, lines landing on it, palm fronds bridging to tile — then walk the roofline and eaves, read the attic for runs, pellets, and rub marks, and finish at ground level: garage seals, AC and pipe penetrations, dumpster and dock areas, pond-facing lot lines. Every entry and every sign gets photographed, and you see the map before we talk about price.

Snap traps and enclosed stations go where the sign says the animals travel — along attic top plates, on enclosure rails, at burrow mouths and pad edges — out of reach of kids and pets, checked and reset until the attic goes quiet and stays quiet. No loose poison in insulation: a rat that dies in a wall void in Florida humidity is a smell and a fly problem, not a solution.

Sealing is matched to the building's era. Bungalows get eave returns and vent openings rebuilt in hardware cloth and flashing, gnawed corners closed in metal, and garage and carriage-house gaps fitted properly. Slab homes get garage door seals that actually meet the apron, utility penetrations collared in gnaw-resistant material instead of foam, and enclosure and equipment gaps screened. You also get the short tree list — the specific limbs breaking the route.

Soiled insulation and nest material hold scent that advertises the attic to the next rat, so contaminated spots get pulled and the area treated once the animals are out. Fallen fruit, outdoor pet food, and pad-side trash get a plain written fix list. Then a recheck on a date, not a promise: we re-walk the roofline and attic, confirm the seals held and the runs are cold, and put it in writing.

lake-buena-vista/termite-control.heroLocal: In Lake Buena Vista a termite call usually starts with a swarm at the lobby lights. The building stock along Hotel Plaza Boulevard and SR-535 went up in the seventies and eighties on flat, sandy, high-water-table ground, and it has been irrigated ever since — turf and mulch held green against stucco walls through every dry season, which means the soil at the slab edge never really dries out. Off Palm Parkway and Apopka-Vineland the same conditions sit under stucco condo and timeshare buildings where a dozen owners share one foundation, and around Lake Bryan they sit under wood-framed houses with docks, decks, and mulch beds against the wall. Different buildings, same setup: warm wet sand, wood or stucco-over-frame above it, and subterranean termites treating the landscaping plan as a dinner invitation.
lake-buena-vista/termite-control.heroService: Termite control in Lake Buena Vista starts with telling you which termite you actually have, because the treatments do not overlap. We inspect the soil line, the slab penetrations, the stacked plumbing walls, the attic, and the wood that touches the ground, then identify the species — Eastern subterranean, Formosan, or drywood — before we quote anything. Subterranean work means a treated zone in the soil or a monitored bait system, plus the moisture and mulch fixes that keep inviting them. Drywood work is localised to the infested wood. Hotels and associations get the findings in a written record with photos, dated, that can go straight into a brand file, an insurance file, or an owner's packet.

body: For the hotels along Hotel Plaza Boulevard, SR-535, and Vineland Avenue, termite work is renovation work whether it is planned or not. These are stucco and block buildings from the first Disney-era building waves, renovated in cycles ever since, and the colonies are most often found when a wall is opened for a remodel — framing already honeycombed behind paint that looked fine. We inspect around that reality: the ground-floor soil line and planters, the expansion joints, the plumbing penetrations where stacked bathrooms rise through the building, and any wall with a leak history, because a chronic condensate or shower leak is exactly where a Formosan aerial colony sets up above the reach of a soil barrier. Findings go into a dated written record with photographs and a treatment map, written so a general manager can hand it to a brand QA inspector, an insurer, or a capital-projects team without translating it. Treatment is phased around occupancy — exterior soil work and bait stations first, interior drilling and wall work scheduled into rooms already out of rotation — so the fix does not take sellable rooms down to get done.

Vacation condos and timeshares off Palm Parkway, Apopka-Vineland, and Lake Bryan's rental streets have a termite problem that is mostly an ownership problem. One slab can carry units owned by people in five states, an association responsible for the grounds, and a manager responsible for the guests, and termites do not care whose budget the trench comes out of. Colonies move along a shared foundation from the unit that ignores them to the unit that just paid for treatment, which is why single-unit termite work in these buildings so often fails. We inspect the building run, not just the reporting unit: the whole soil line, the shared walls, the utility entries, and the landscape beds the association maintains. The report is written per building with a per-unit summary, so an off-site owner gets a document that explains what was found under their unit, what the treatment covers, and what the association still needs to fix — usually mulch over the screed, irrigation overspray on the walls, and wood-to-ground contacts nobody has owned in years.

Around Lake Bryan and the residential pockets behind the resort corridors, the termite pressure is the classic Florida residential pattern with a waterfront multiplier. Houses sit on damp ground near the lake, docks and boathouses put treated-but-ageing timber in and near the water, and decks, fences, and pergolas give subterraneans above-ground feeding stations that bridge straight toward the house. Inside, the risk points are the quiet ones: the tub and shower walls, the AC condensate line that drips at the foundation, the garage slab joint, and the planter built against the stucco. We walk the lot as well as the house — dock timber, fence lines, wood storage, tree stumps — because a colony eating a dock this year is scouting the house next year. Treatment pairs a soil barrier or bait system with the specific wood-to-ground fixes your lot needs, and the annual re-inspection checks the waterfront wood first, not last.
localSection.heading: Seventies hotels, shared-foundation condos, and lake houses on Lake Bryan

pests.blurb: The native Florida subterranean and still the most common find in Lake Buena Vista. Colonies work from nests in the damp soil up mud tubes the width of a pencil into slab cracks, plumbing penetrations, and stucco edges, eating the soft spring wood and leaving paint and a paper-thin veneer intact — which is why a door frame can look perfect and crush like a shell. They swarm on warm spring days, usually March through May, shedding wings on windowsills and porches. Finding swarmers indoors means the colony is feeding on the building, not passing through. We confirm the entry points, treat the soil zone they travel through, and fix the moisture and mulch conditions that let them establish.
pests.name: Eastern Subterranean Termites

pests.blurb: The species that changes the conversation. Formosan colonies are far larger than Eastern ones — millions of workers, foraging over a wide area — and they swarm at dusk in late spring, drawn to light in numbers that can coat a lobby entrance or a porch fixture. Worse, Formosans can cut their soil connection and live as aerial nests in a wet wall or roof, fed by a plumbing or condensate leak, where a ground treatment alone never touches them. In stacked hotel and condo plumbing walls that leak history matters as much as the soil line. We inspect for aerial nests wherever moisture has been chronic, treat the soil and the nest, and put the leak on the written fix list — leave the water, and you keep the termites.
pests.name: Formosan Subterranean Termites

pests.blurb: Drywoods live inside the wood itself — no soil, no mud tubes — and in a resort corridor they often arrive inside it: infested furniture, picture frames, and wood fixtures moved from unit to unit and property to property. The sign is frass, tiny hard pellets like ground pepper or sand pushed out of pinholes onto a sill or a desk, and wood that sounds papery when tapped. A hotel desk or a condo's wood trim can carry a small colony for years. Because the colony is confined to the piece, the honest treatment is localised — treat or remove the infested wood — not a building-wide tenting quote, unless inspection shows it has spread into structural framing. We identify exactly which pieces are active before anyone pays to treat the ones that are not.
pests.name: Drywood Termites in Furniture and Trim

pests.blurb: Every spring and early summer, Lake Buena Vista's first termite evidence arrives on the wing. Subterranean swarmers pour out on warm humid evenings after rain — Formosans after dusk around lights, Easterns more often in daytime — and pile up at lobby glass, pool fixtures, porch lights, and bright windows, leaving drifts of identical shed wings. Guests and owners regularly mistake them for flying ants; the difference is in the wings (four equal wings that drop off, versus an ant's two uneven pairs) and a straight, bead-like body with no pinched waist. A swarm outdoors near lights is a warning. A swarm emerging indoors, or wings on interior sills, means a colony is feeding on the building itself. Photograph them, save a few in a bag, and call — identification from the swarmers alone tells us which species and how urgent the inspection is.
pests.name: Swarmers at the Lights

pests.blurb: An honest termite call in Florida starts with the look-alikes. Carpenter ants swarm too, hollow out wet wood for nesting rather than food, and leave coarse sawdust with insect parts in it, not termite frass. Powderpost beetles push fine powder from pinholes in hardwoods and bamboo. Wood-decay fungus softens dock, deck, and bathroom-floor wood until it feels exactly like termite damage to a thumb, and old, inactive mud tubes from a colony treated years ago can sit harmless in a garage for a decade. Each one is a different fix at a different price, and treating for termites you do not have wastes all of it. We identify what is actually in the wood — frass shape, tube structure, the gallery pattern inside — and say so plainly before anything is sold.
pests.name: When It Is Not Termites at All

process.detail: We inspect by building type: hotels get the soil line, planters, expansion joints, and stacked plumbing walls checked, plus any leak-history wall opened to a moisture meter; condos get the full building run and shared foundation; houses get the lot too — dock, deck, fence, and wood storage. Every tube, swarm site, and damaged piece is photographed, and the species is identified from soldiers, swarmers, frass, and gallery pattern before any treatment is proposed.

Subterranean colonies are treated where they travel: a liquid termiticide zone trenched and rodded around the slab and at penetrations, or a monitored bait system where landscaping, pavers, or a pool deck make trenching the wrong tool — Formosan aerial nests get treated directly in the wall as well, because soil work cannot reach them. Drywood colonies confined to furniture or trim are treated locally or the piece is removed. You see the treatment map and know which method is on your building and why.

Treatment without correction is a subscription. You get a short written list, specific to your building: irrigation heads soaking the foundation wall, mulch raked over the weep screed, the condensate line dripping at the slab, planters and wood structures touching stucco, the shower leak feeding the wall. For hotels and associations the list names which items are the property's and which are the association's, so it can actually be acted on. We re-check the list at the annual inspection.
process.step: The moisture and wood-to-ground fix list

process.detail: Termite protection here is a document as much as a treatment. Hotels get the dated inspection and treatment record for the brand and insurance file; condo owners get the per-unit summary for a property they may not visit this year; homeowners get the damage map and the treatment warranty terms in plain writing. The annual re-inspection re-walks the soil line, bait stations, plumbing walls, and waterfront wood, and reports what changed — because in Lake Buena Vista the question is never whether termites are nearby, only whether they have found your building yet.
